Update holdings from a Nordnet export

In Nordnet, open Innehav, print the page to PDF, and choose that PDF here. It is read in this browser only: the PDF itself is not uploaded anywhere, and the only thing saved is each holding's name, quantity and value. Sold stocks move to Former holdings on the Strategy tab, new ones are matched to their listing automatically, and the whole board is rebuilt in about 15–20 minutes.

Portfolio breakdown

Money flow is the board's own reading (see "Where money is moving"): for sector, industry group and industry slices it is the money flow in that sector or industry in its home market, for every other slicing it is the money flow in the stocks themselves. A slice's score is the average of its holdings' scores (-7.5 to +7.5) weighted by value; +1.5 or more reads as money coming in, -1.5 or less as money leaving, and beyond 4.5 as strong. Holdings with no flow reading are left out of the average. Sector, industry group and industry use the standard GICS names; they are TradingView's industry labels translated to GICS, with a short list of well-known companies set by hand where the two differ, so a few companies may sit one industry off. Country is where the company is based or incorporated (Medtronic and Eaton are Irish-domiciled). Funds are placed by the theme they track. Amounts are the latest price times your quantity.

Short term against long term

Each circle is a holding, sized by its value. Right means stronger October signals, up means a better outlook over the horizon you pick. Hover for details, click to open it in the table.

Sell or add by December

Each holding is scored on four things: whether money is entering or leaving its sector in its own market (for an ETF, the companies it holds most of), its October signal, its 1-year outlook, and its own money flow. The lowest scores are flagged to consider selling or trimming, the highest to consider adding. These are signals to weigh, not instructions. In an ISK, selling has no tax effect either way. Click a holding to see it in full.

      Every holding

      Click a column to sort and a row to see every indicator for that holding. Prices are in each listing's own currency. Money flow ranks each stock against its own market to 16 October: its 12-month trend counts three parts, heavy-volume buying over 60 days and 20-day Chaikin money flow one part each; "strong" is the top or bottom 10% with at least 20 million kronor traded a day.

      Signal. Alert buy appears when the 50-day average is about to touch the 200-day from below, and Alert sell when it is about to touch it from above. "About to touch" means within 1% of the 200-day and closing in so that, at its pace over the last 5 sessions, it would meet it within 10 trading days. An alert stays for 7 trading days after the last session that met this (so it also covers the touch itself) unless the averages cross the other way. The rest of the time the column shows the strategy view behind the December column: Strong buy (consider adding), Buy (hold, add on dips), Hold, Sell (consider trimming) and Strong sell (consider selling). Not advice on what to buy or sell.

      Candle touch. Alert buy in blue: regular when the daily candle touches the 200-day average upwards (comes up from below and its high reaches it) and finishes the day on the upper side of it; bold when it touches the 50-day average downwards (comes down from above and its low reaches it), finishes the day above the 50-day, and the 50-day is above the 200-day. Alert sell in orange: regular when the candle touches the 200-day downwards and finishes the day below it; bold when it touches the 50-day upwards, finishes the day below it, and the 50-day is below the 200-day. Each alert is kept for 5 sessions after its candle unless a newer one appears; a dash otherwise. "From above" and "from below" are judged against the previous close.

      Strongest bullish readings by market

      A rules-based screen of the biggest listed companies in each market, ranked by how many of 13 published TradingView readings point up. It is not a recommendation to buy or sell anything and says nothing about what a stock will do next. These stocks are not your holdings. Prices come straight from TradingView in your browser (15 minutes delayed) and refresh every 5 minutes. Before the US market opens, stocks with a pre-market quote show that price (marked "pre") and the move against the last close.

      How the ranking works
      • Universe: common stocks listed in the market and based in that country (cross-listings are left out; when a company has several share classes, the one traded most is kept).
      • Large caps: the 30 biggest companies on each market by market value (so "large" is relative to that market; in smaller markets these include companies that would be mid-sized elsewhere). Mid caps (the next 40, ranks 31 to 70) appear only if they reach a score of 85 or more, and at most 3 of the 10 places go to mid caps. Smaller companies are not screened.
      • Each company gets one point for every reading below that is true. A reading with no data earns nothing and is left out of the maximum; companies with fewer than 8 readings available are skipped.
      • Trend: price above its 50-day average; price above its 200-day average; 50-day above 200-day.
      • Momentum: RSI between 50 and 75; MACD above its signal line; up over 1 month; up over 3 months; ADX at least 20 with +DI above −DI.
      • Money flow: Chaikin money flow above zero (20 days).
      • Analysts and fundamentals: average analyst rating 2.0 or better (1 = strong buy, 5 = sell); average price target at least 10% above the price; revenue growing year on year; net margin above zero.
      • The score uses TradingView's last official close and its daily indicators, not pre-market quotes, because those trade thinly; the pre-market price is shown beside it for reference.
      • Score = points earned divided by readings available, as a number out of 100. The 10 highest scores per market are listed, strongest first; ties go to the larger company.

        How the signals are worked out

        October signal. Each holding gets a point for each bullish reading and loses one for each bearish reading, on daily bars: RSI(14) between 55 and 75 or below 45; MACD(12,26,9) above or below its signal line and moving the same way; price above or below both the 20- and 50-day averages; the Williams Alligator eating up or down; price above the top or below the bottom of this month's CPR; buying or selling pressure (Chaikin money flow over 20 days together with up/down volume); higher highs and lows or lower highs and lows; and a break above or below the 55-day range. Bollinger bands riding the upper or lower band and a bullish or bearish candlestick pattern in the last three days count half a point. A total of 4 or more is Bullish, 1.5 to 4 Mildly bullish, −1.5 to 1.5 Neutral, −4 to −1.5 Mildly bearish and −4 or lower Bearish.

        Monthly CPR is the central pivot range for October, built from September's high, low and close. Trading above its top is read as bullish for the month, below its bottom as bearish. R1 and S1 are the first resistance and support levels.

        Outlook over 1, 3 and 5 years. Each horizon is a score that weighs different evidence, sorted into the same five groups (Positive at +3.5 or more, Leaning positive from +1, Mixed between, Leaning negative from −1, Negative at −3.5 or less). 1 year leans on what tends to persist for months: price against the 40-week average and whether that average is rising, weekly MACD, the last 6 months against the S&P 500 or OMX Stockholm, a small share of the October score, a penalty for being more than half below the 52-week high, revenue and earnings growth, and the analyst consensus and average target. 3 years leans on the business: revenue growth (the biggest weight), earnings growth, net margin, free cash flow, return on equity, debt to equity and the P/E, with a light weight on the weekly trend and analysts. 5 years leans on durability: profitability, return on equity, free cash flow, gross margin, whether revenue is growing or shrinking, debt, how much growth the valuation already assumes, and size (under $1B counts against, over $50B for). ETFs are scored on trend only, with a small credit at 3 and 5 years for spreading company risk; holdings with no fundamentals in TradingView's screener are Mixed at 3 and 5 years. These are rules of thumb built from current data, not forecasts: no one predicts 5-year returns reliably, and the further out the horizon, the more the score describes the business rather than the share price.

        Where money is moving. There is no public record of what institutions buy day to day, so the board infers it from trading. To choose how, the ways of reading flows were tested on four years of daily bars for about 1,300 stocks in the US, Sweden, Norway, Europe and Canada: every week each sector was scored, and the score was checked against how the sector then did against its own market over the next one and three months. The method was chosen on the period up to mid-2025 and confirmed on the 14 months since, which it had not seen. The reading that held up best is the sector's 12-month trend with the last month left out (the average of its companies), counted three parts, plus its heavy-volume buying over the last 60 days, counted one part: big investors build and cut positions over months, so their buying shows up as a lasting trend more reliably than in any one week's volume. Each sector is ranked against the others in its market (US companies worth over $2 billion; the biggest Swedish, Norwegian and Canadian companies; European companies worth over $5 billion, plus Danish and Finnish companies). Denmark, Finland, Germany and Canada also have their own chart, each ranked among that market's largest companies (about 70, 80, 110 and 130 by market value, one share class per company), with sectors of at least three companies: the top sixth reads as strong inflow, the top third as money coming in, the bottom third as money leaving and the bottom sixth as strong outflow, with the score running from −7.5 to +7.5. On the unseen period, sectors in the top sixth beat their market over the next one to three months 56% of the time and those in the bottom sixth lagged it 57% of the time; the earlier volume-first reading was right 50% to 52% of the time, close to a coin toss. Holdings are matched to their industry where at least six (US and Europe) or four (Sweden and Norway) companies share it, otherwise to their sector, with the same four hand matches as before. Danish, Finnish and German holdings keep their reading against European large caps; on their home market's chart they count towards the “what you hold” figure only.

        Money flow in each stock. Each holding is ranked against the stocks of its own market by the stock reading that tested best on the same data: its 12-month trend with the last month left out, counted three parts; heavy-volume buying, the days in the last 60 when volume beat its 50-day average and the stock closed in the upper part of its range, minus those when it closed in the lower part, one part; and 20-day Chaikin money flow, one part. Fourteen other measures were tested alone and together, among them big-volume days, volume surges, on-balance volume, up/down volume, money flow index, force index and VWAP; on the unseen period the short-term volume readings on their own were right about half the time. The rank sets the label: top 10% strong inflow, next 10% money coming in, bottom 10% strong outflow, next 10% money leaving; "strong" also needs at least 20 million kronor traded a day, about the size where institutions can build or cut a position. The score runs from −7.5 to +7.5 (the rank, centred). On the unseen period, the top 10% beat their market over the next three months 54% of the time and the bottom 10% lagged it 53% of the time; the earlier six-part volume reading was right about 51% of the time. Below 1 million kronor traded a day a holding is marked too thinly traded to tell, and with less than a year of history too new to tell. For ETFs this reads the fund's own price and trading on Xetra, ranked against European stocks.

        Stocks under each sector. Only the sector's most-traded 40% are considered, so the names are ones institutions actually trade, each read with the same stock ranking as your holdings; where a company has two share classes, only one is shown. Your ETFs' look-through flow is the average stock reading of each fund's biggest holdings, weighted as in the fund.

        Sell or add by December. Four parts, with money flow weighted most: the money-flow score of the holding's sector or industry divided by 2.5 (up to ±2); the stock's own money-flow score divided by 2.5 (up to ±2, left out when it is too thinly traded or too new to tell); the October score divided by 3 (up to ±1.5); and the 1-year outlook score divided by 2 (up to ±1.5). A total of −3.5 or less is flagged to consider selling by December, down to −2 to consider trimming, +2 or more to hold and add on dips, and +4 or more to consider adding if the 1-year outlook is positive and the 5-year outlook is not negative. For ETFs the sector part is the flow into the fund's ten biggest holdings, and the Saturna fund is held back from "adding" because of its size and cost.

        ETF facts. Holdings, costs, sizes and longer-run returns come from VanEck, iShares and State Street fact sheets, WisdomTree, etf.capital, Trackinsight and finanzfluss, each dated on its card. The Saturna fund's top holdings are approximate, from Halal Terminal, because the issuer page was not available. Overlaps use only each fund's top 10, so real overlaps are somewhat larger.

        One-year range and buy-price check. The typical yearly swing is each holding's volatility over the last 252 trading days (for 2020 Bulkers, only since its May 2026 special dividend). The middle half and 8-in-10 ranges assume it keeps swinging that much with no trend up or down, so they show how far the price could plausibly be from today in a year, not a forecast. The buy-price check uses the same assumption for its chance of being above your price, then sorts the result into four groups with the 1-year outlook. Your buy price is only used in this page while it is open and is not saved.

        Monthly likely low and high. For each month-end from October 2026 to October 2027, the likely low and likely high are the 25th and 75th percentile prices: half of outcomes fall between them, a quarter below and a quarter above. The gap widens with the square root of time, so a holding with a 40% yearly swing sits within roughly ±14% after three months and ±27% after a year. Real prices jump around earnings and news, so actual paths are lumpier than these smooth bands.

        Most likely price and the bold side. The most likely price is the middle of the range after a modest tilt: today's price grown at 5% a year (roughly stocks' long-run average) plus 1.5 percentage points for each point of the holding's 1-year outlook score, capped at ±10, so between −5% and +15% a year. With that tilt, the chance of ending at or above the likely high and at or below the likely low are no longer equal; the larger one is in bold. The tilt is a judgment: trends and fundamentals have only a weak record of predicting one-year returns, so it is kept small, and for very volatile holdings the two chances stay close to 25% each.

        Automatic updates and former holdings. Every weekday morning, and whenever you update your holdings, the board is rebuilt from scratch on GitHub: about 1,600 companies' daily bars from Yahoo Finance and their sector, fundamentals and analyst data from TradingView's screener, for your holdings, the stocks you used to own and the eight markets' money flow. The technical readings follow the rules above; checked against the board's original readings for 102 holdings, the rebuild gives the same October signal for 94, the same MACD, Alligator, Bollinger and price-structure reading for 93 to 100, and RSI and moving-average distances within a point or two for all but one or two. The 1-, 3- and 5-year outlooks use weights recovered from the original scores (same group for 83 to 85% of holdings, never more than one group apart), so treat them as approximate. The detail panel's notes on news stay as written. Former holdings are every stock that was on the board and is not any more, dated by the first Nordnet export it was missing from.

        Candle touch column. Alert buy in regular blue means the daily candle touched the 200-day moving average upwards: the previous close was below it, the day's high reached it, and the day finished above it. Alert buy in bold blue means the candle touched the 50-day average downwards (previous close above it, the low reached it), closed the day above it, and the 50-day is above the 200-day, so a dip in an uptrend. Alert sell in regular orange is the mirror image on the 200-day (previous close above it, the low reached it, and the day finished below it), and bold orange means the candle touched the 50-day upwards (previous close below it, the high reached it), closed below it, and the 50-day is below the 200-day, a rally in a downtrend. An alert is kept for 5 sessions after the candle, or until a newer alert replaces it; if both averages are touched the same day, both are shown. While TradingView's live prices are on (every minute), today's candle counts as it develops, so an alert can appear or disappear during the day until the close settles it; the stored history comes from the daily rebuild.

        Signal column. Alert buy means the 50-day moving average is about to touch the 200-day from below (a golden cross is near) and Alert sell that it is about to touch it from above (a death cross is near). The test: the gap between them is under 1% of the 200-day, the 50-day has been on the same side for 6 sessions, and it has been closing in fast enough that, at its pace over the last 5 sessions, it would touch within 10 trading days. The alert is kept for 7 trading days after the last session that met the test, which also covers the cross itself, unless the averages cross the other way. The live prices are checked every minute, so an alert can appear before the daily rebuild. Otherwise the column translates the strategy view in the December column: Consider adding is Strong buy, Hold with adding on dips is Buy, Hold stays Hold, Consider trimming is Sell and Consider selling is Strong sell. A moving-average approach often fizzles out (the averages can turn away before touching), and a cross is a slow signal that comes after much of the move.

        Limits. Indicators describe the trend and momentum so far; they do not predict prices, and a two-week window is mostly noise. Analyst targets can lag sharp falls, so a large upside to target often means the target has not been cut yet. Earnings reports in late October and early November can override any of these readings. The money-flow readings tilt the odds rather than confirm what institutions did: even the best method tested was right only 53% to 57% of the time, and reported holdings arrive months later in quarterly filings.
